name: Fatima Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 27, and I'm a junior at Crescent Accounts, a firm of seven on the busy shopping street, near the mosque and the market. Most of our clients are family businesses: grocers, restaurants, a tailor, taxi drivers. I'm married to Yusuf, who repairs phones and laptops from a stall in the market, and we rent a flat above a sweet shop. We have about three weeks of money saved, because we sent a lot to his parents for his father's operation last spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do bookkeeping, VAT returns and year-end accounts, and in January it's all taxi drivers' tax returns. I use AI tools every day: to turn photos of receipts into spreadsheets, to draft letters to the tax office, and to explain rules in Urdu or Arabic for clients who prefer it. I love that clients trust me like family, aunties bring me samosas. What wears me out is that I'm still weak on the technical side, and Mr Siddiqui, the owner, has to correct my work on anything complicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but it's not magic, and the people selling it oversold it. At work I'd say we should keep using it for the receipts and letters, it saves us hours. In the family group chat I'd tell my cousins to stop worrying about robots and study properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit disappointing, because I was hoping the tools would let me take on far more clients. My job's safe enough, but my money isn't, because my pay's low and we've hardly any savings since the operation. There are only a couple of other firms nearby that serve our community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the technical rules, VAT and property income mainly, so Mr Siddiqui trusts me with bigger clients. I'd keep using AI for the routine bits so I can handle more taxi drivers in January. And I'd start a small side service doing bookkeeping for two market stallholders, maybe £200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The AI's fine, it's the bank balance and Yusuf's quiet months that bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are Yusuf's quiet months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After Christmas, January and February are thin. In January and February nobody's buying phone cases or getting screens fixed, so my husband Yusuf and I eat a lot of lentils. Last year he made about half his usual money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Siddiqui mind your side service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him first, of course, it's his firm and his name. The stallholders are too small for Crescent anyway, they'd pay £50 a month at most. He'd probably say fine, as long as I don't take his clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small firms that move quickly, and I'd say it with a smile. At work I'd tell Mr Siddiqui we should offer cheaper packages to the community using these tools. In the family chat I'd tell the young ones to learn the tools and a trade, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mostly good for me, as long as I'm the one using the tools and not the one replaced by them. A lot of my routine work goes, but clients here want someone who speaks their language and knows their family. If Crescent needs fewer people, I think Mr Siddiqui keeps the one who brings in the aunties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd propose a cheaper AI-assisted package for small shops and taxi drivers, with me running it. I'd take a course on the cloud accounting software. And I'd grow my side bookkeeping to five stallholders, so we're not relying on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It feels like a door opening, if I walk through it fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a risk the clients just use the software themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will, the younger ones. But Mr Akhtar the grocer still brings his receipts in a carrier bag and wants to drink tea while I explain. People like him trust a face, not an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says this will cost jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, some, and people should learn rather than complain. My dad lost his factory job at 45 and started driving a taxi, and nobody gave him anything. He just got on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and families and communities need to pull together. At work I'd say we must look after our clients, they'll be scared too. At the mosque I'd help organise something, maybe advice sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone soon after 2028, because it's all thinking work, and the AI can speak Urdu too. Being early with the AI tools doesn't matter if the tools don't need me. Yusuf's repair work is hands-on, so he's got until about 2031 before robots, and that's our three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save everything, cut the visits and the eating out, aim for two months. I'd go into business with Yusuf, doing his books and growing the stall into a small shop, because hands-on repair lasts longer. Once AGI arrived, I'd lean on family and the community, and help others do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel the ground going, but I'd keep busy, because keeping busy is how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we had to, yes, but family first, that's how we do it. My brothers would help, and we'd help them. The government's slow, family's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're fine and we have a plan, even if the plan is thin. My mum would say pray and work. She'd be right on both counts.

say: I'd say it's frightening, and families and **communities** need to pull together.
I'd help organise **advice sessions** at the mosque for scared clients.
think: My job's **gone soon after 2028**; the AI can speak Urdu too.

fieldNote: Sees her language skills are **no shield** against AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning and we should use it. At work I'd say let's become the firm the community trusts for everything, tax, benefits, business advice. At the mosque I'd set up a small evening class on the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to build my own little practice before 2031. And Yusuf can grow the repair shop until the robots come around 2034. It's a lot of change, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, finish my exams so I'm properly qualified. By year two, I'd start my own small bookkeeping practice for stallholders and taxi drivers, using AI for the routine work. We'd save £150 a month for Yusuf's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan and plenty to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting a practice with three weeks of savings, is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not alone, so I'd keep my job at Crescent part-time while the practice grows. My brother would lend us something if we needed it. Small steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted children in two or three years. We'd still want them, but maybe wait till the shop's steady. Children are a blessing, not a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. At work I'd tell Mr Siddiqui to plan for the firm's future now. In the community I'd run classes on the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be fine. I'd be 37 with my own practice, Yusuf with a shop, and maybe children. My accounting tasks go in 2036, but I'd have ten years to become the person the community comes to for any money question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, qualify. Then build my practice slowly, ten clients, then thirty, using AI for the routine work. We'd save toward buying the flat, maybe by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like an opportunity, if we work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you not calm, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something happened with family again, like another operation. Another family operation is the thing that wipes us out, not AI. Health, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be left behind, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older aunties and uncles who won't touch a phone. I'd want to make sure they have someone to help them. That might even be my business.

I'd tell Mr Siddiqui to plan the **firm's future** now, not later.
think: I think we'd be **fine**, with my practice and Yusuf's shop.
I'd become the person for **any money question** in the community.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to build anything and we've almost no savings. What would help is small business loans with low interest, so people like Yusuf and me could start something. And training in our own languages for the older people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about language. A lot of my clients prefer to talk about money in Urdu, and they trust me because of it. If AI can speak Urdu too, it's not just my job that changes, it's how my whole community does business.

headlineQuote: If AI can speak Urdu too, it's not just my job that changes, it's how my whole community does business.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old **junior** at a seven-person firm serving her **community's** family businesses.
Married to Yusuf, a **phone repairer**, she has three weeks saved after a family operation.
Traditional and adaptive, she uses **AI daily** and plans her own small practice.
She's uneasy in milder scenarios, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and **calm** with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to build and almost no **savings**.
whatWouldHelp: **Low-interest business loans** for people starting something.
Training in **their own languages** for older people.
